title: Zaynab bint Jahsh
hookLine: the wives measure their hands to solve a riddle, and the answer turns out to be charity (Muslim)

cards: Who will be first? In Sahih Muslim, Aisha tells it. The Prophet had said to his wives that the one of them with the longest hand would be the quickest to join him after his death.
So they measured their hands, side by side, to see whose was longest. It sounds like a party game: wives holding out their arms, comparing fingertips. And they missed what he meant.

teach.b: The wives took the words of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, literally, and looked for the longest arm.
But Aisha says the longest hand among them was Zaynab bint Jahsh's, because she used to work with her hands and give in charity. Tradition says she was the first of the wives to follow him in death.
The riddle was never about length. It was about reach: how far a person's hands went toward others. In Arabic the phrase is atwalukunna yadan, the longest of you in hand.
The report itself shows what a long hand meant: a giving one. Notice where her giving came from. Zaynab didn't only hand over what she had.
She made things, the report says, and gave from the work of her own hands.

teach.h: A LONG HAND IS A GENEROUS ONE.
teach.b: Charity that has your fingerprints on it. Notice also who tells us this. Aisha and Zaynab were rivals in the household; the reports don't hide it.

Yet it is Aisha who preserves Zaynab's best memory. In another report in Muslim, Aisha describes her as unmatched in her religion, in her fear of Allah, in truthfulness, in keeping ties of family, and in giving charity.
And in the account of the slander against Aisha, Bukhari has Zaynab asked what she knew, and answering that she knew nothing but good of her.

teach.h: RIVALS WHO SPOKE WELL OF EACH OTHER.
teach.b: The two women spoke well of each other when it counted.
The longest hands, it turns out, also reached across a rivalry.

how: Muslims retell the hadith of 'the longest hand' from Sahih Muslim when speaking of charity, and honor Zaynab bint Jahsh among the mothers of the believers for giving from the work of her hands.

o: the one of you with the most children
the strongest of you in battle and in work
the longest of you in hand: the most giving

games.q: Zaynab bint Jahsh — tap the pairs.
p: the one who gave the most
worked with her hands and gave

s: the longest hand meant the longest arm
Aisha says it meant Zaynab, who worked with her hands and gave in charity.
Aisha and Zaynab spoke well of each other
Aisha praised Zaynab's charity, and Zaynab said she knew only good of Aisha.
Zaynab gave only from wealth she was given
the report says she worked with her own hands and gave from that.

games.q: the Prophet says the wife with the longest hand will follow him first. you and the others want to know who it is. what do you do?
o: measure your hands against each other's.
games.why: Aisha says they measured, and only later understood it meant Zaynab, the most giving.

practice: Rest your hands open on your knees, and look at them.

Think of one thing they could make or do for someone else, bake something, mend something, write a note by hand, carry someone's bags, something with your fingerprints on it, and picture your hands doing it.
If you pray, ask that your hands reach a little further.

wordCard.voice: Atwalukunna yadan, 'the longest of you in hand,' the riddle about reach, not length, that named Zaynab bint Jahsh, who gave from her own hands' work. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: 'the longest of you in hand', the Prophet's words in Muslim.

carryVoice: Your line: the longest hands. Reach, not length, and across a rivalry too. That's day eight hundred twelve.
